e.etymology: A short form of Frederick (Germanic for peace and ruler), and also of Alfred and Wilfred. It was a top American name in its own right in the late 1800s.
namesakes: Fred Rogers (host of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood)
Fred Weasley (one of the Weasley twins in Harry Potter)

assoc.t: Fred Jones, leader of the Scooby-Doo gang

e.etymology: The Italian short form of Eleonora, a cousin of Eleanor, a name of uncertain origin from medieval Provence. Leonora is the heroine of Verdi's operas Il trovatore and La forza del destino.
From Arabic sana, brilliance or splendor. In Swahili the word sanaa means art, which is how some American families read the name.
namesakes: Sanaa Lathan (actress in Love and Basketball)

e.etymology: From malina, the word for raspberry in Polish and other Slavic languages. Malina is also the name of the sun goddess in Inuit tradition.
From Germanic words for fame and ruler. The medieval name was revived after Walter Scott used it in a poem in 1811, and it also serves as the English form of Scottish Ruairidh and Welsh Rhydderch.
namesakes: Roderick Usher (doomed heir in Poe's The Fall of the House of Usher)

e.etymology: From Latin silva, forest, by way of Silvanus, the Roman god of woods, and French Sylvain. Sylvan is also the English adjective for anything wooded.
The Spanish form of Amber, the golden fossil resin, a word that goes back to Arabic anbar. A separate Indian name Ambar, used for boys, comes from Sanskrit ambara, sky.

e.meaning: uncertain; champion and cloud are the usual suggestions
e.etymology: From Old Irish Niall, a name so old that its meaning was lost; champion and cloud are the usual guesses. Niall of the Nine Hostages was a legendary high king of Ireland. Neil is the same name.
e.note: In Ireland it is usually NYE-ul; Americans often guess nee-ALL from the spelling.

assoc.t: Niall Horan, singer formerly of One Direction

e.etymology: A spelling of Raya, a name with several sources, among them a Hebrew word for friend or companion and a Slavic short form of Raisa. Raya rose after Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon (2021).

assoc.t: heroine of Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon (as Raya)

e.meaning: dweller in or near the woods
e.etymology: An English surname for someone who lived in or by a wood. It has recently joined Brooks, Banks and Hayes among surnames ending in s used as first names.

A spelling of Rip, an old nickname best known from Rip Van Winkle. It came into use as a given name after Rip Wheeler, the ranch foreman in the TV series Yellowstone (2018). Ripp is also a German and English surname.

assoc.t: Rip Wheeler of the TV series Yellowstone (as Rip)
Rip Van Winkle, Washington Irving's sleeper (as Rip)

e.note: Sounds the same as rip, to tear, and reads like RIP, rest in peace.

e.etymology: A spelling of Teagan, from the Irish surname O Tadhgain, descendant of Tadhgan, a pet form of Tadhg, poet. Some connect it to the Welsh name Tegan instead, from teg, fair.
The Spanish form of Jacob, from Latin Iacobus and Hebrew Yaakov, traditionally explained as holder of the heel or supplanter. Santiago, Jaime and Yago are other Spanish forms of the same name.
An Italian form of Cosimo, from St. Cosmas, a 4th-century martyr whose name is Greek kosmos, order or the ordered universe. A Scottish ducal family brought it from Italy to Britain in the 1700s.

assoc.t: the cosmopolitan cocktail, called a cosmo
Cosmo, fairy godparent on The Fairly OddParents
Cosmo the Spacedog in Guardians of the Galaxy

e.etymology: In the US a modern name in the sound family of Avion and Aviana. It matches the English word avian, of birds, from Latin avis. An old Russian church name is also written Avian.
e.note: Avian is the ordinary English word for anything to do with birds, as in avian flu.

e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Gabriel, from gever, strong man or hero, and El, God. In the Bible Gabriel is the angel who carries God's messages.
A spelling of Messiah, from Hebrew mashiach, anointed one, the promised deliverer in Judaism and the title Christians give to Jesus. Massiah is also a Caribbean surname.
e.note: Messiah is a religious title, and some people object to it as a child's name.

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins Jah-, as in Jahmir and Jahlil, to Kai. Jah is a short form of the Hebrew name of God and is familiar from Rastafari and reggae.
Coined in 18th-century England by adding the -inda ending of Belinda and Lucinda to the Mel- of names such as Melissa and Melanie. It was most popular in the US in the 1960s and 1970s.
namesakes: Melinda French Gates (philanthropist and co-founder of the Gates Foundation)

e.meaning: from Airelle, a place in Normandy
e.etymology: A spelling of Darrell, a surname from the Norman family d'Airel, named for Airelle in Normandy. It became a first name in the 19th century and was most popular in the US in the 1960s.
namesakes: Darryl Philbin (warehouse foreman on The Office)
Darryl McDaniels (DMC of the rap group Run-DMC)

e.etymology: A pet form of Don and Donald, from Scottish Gaelic Domhnall, world ruler, and also of Donovan. It has been registered as a full name in the US since the early 1900s.
namesakes: Donnie Wahlberg (New Kids on the Block singer and Blue Bloods actor)
Donnie Darko (title character of the 2001 cult film)

e.etymology: A surname from the Latin genitive of Jacobus, meaning (son) of Jacob. As a first name it is used in the same way as Jacoby, which rose in the US in the 2000s.
An Armenian name borne by a legendary patriarch of the nation. In the Bible Aram is a son of Shem and the land of the Arameans; the Hebrew name is usually linked to a word for high ground.
An elaboration of Ariana with the -ny ending popular in Caribbean Spanish naming. Ariana is a form of Ariadne, from Greek words meaning most holy.
A modern Indian name ending in -ansh, from Sanskrit amsha, a part or portion, like Reyansh and Shivansh. The first element is explained in more than one way.
An English surname from the Old English personal name Cynesige, from cyne, royal, and sige, victory.
namesakes: Kinsey Millhone (detective in Sue Grafton's alphabet mysteries)

assoc.t: Alfred Kinsey, sex researcher behind the Kinsey scale

e.note: Many adults will think of Alfred Kinsey and the Kinsey scale of sexual orientation.

e.etymology: A spelling of Anneliese, the German compound of Anna, grace, and Liese, a short form of Elisabeth, God is my oath.

e.meaning: fiery one, by association with Latin ignis
e.etymology: From the Roman family name Egnatius, of unknown and perhaps Etruscan origin, later respelled to echo Latin ignis, fire. Borne by St. Ignatius of Antioch and St. Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits.
namesakes: Ignatius of Loyola (saint who founded the Jesuits)
Ignatius J. Reilly (hero of the novel A Confederacy of Dunces)

e.etymology: A Slavic feminine form of John, written Yana from Russian, Ukrainian and Bulgarian. It is a cousin of Jana and Jane and goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A Scottish and northern English surname from rivers and places called Calder, a Celtic name built from words for hard and water.

assoc.t: Alexander Calder, sculptor who invented the mobile
Calder Trophy, the NHL's rookie of the year award

e.etymology: A modern American name that joins Ada to the -leigh ending, or respells Adalee. It sits in the same sound family as Adelaide, Adeline and Adalyn.
A modern Hebrew name from the root r-n-n, to sing or shout for joy, related to the Hebrew name Ron. It is close in sound to the Irish name Ronan, which is unrelated.
